He describes a sword that he likened to rainwater in its whiteness and clarity. It was named "raj'" just as "irb" was named, the poet said:

*"Dry, north wind, which does not shelter, because of its scarcity, except the cloud and the 'irb' and the 'sabal'"*

This is naming by the verbal noun of "aba" and "raja'a." The Arabs claim that the cloud carries water from the seas of the earth and then returns it to the earth, when they wish to make an omen, and they named it "raj'" and "irb" so that it would return and come back. It was said: because God, may He be exalted, returns it time after time. al-Khansa said:

*"Like the raj' in the cloudy, flowing night"*

It was said: "al-raj'" means the angels, who were named so because of their returning with the deeds of the servants. It was said: the clouds. The well-known view among lexicographers, and the view of the majority, is that "al-raj'" is rain, and "al-sad'" is what the earth splits open to produce of plants. This suits the view of those who said "al-raj'" is rain. Ibn Zayd said: "dhat al-inshiqaq" (possessing splitting) means plants. He also said: "dhat al-harth" (possessing tillage). Mujahid said: "al-sad'" is what is in the earth of cracks, ditches, trenches, and fissures by tillage and other things, and these are matters in which there is a lesson. From him also: "dhat al-turuq" (possessing paths), which are split by walkers. It was said: "dhat al-amwat" (possessing the dead), because the earth splits open to release them on the Day of Resurrection.

The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ (indeed it) — they said — refers to the Qur'an. (Decisive) ﴿fasl﴾ means it separates between truth and falsehood, just as it has been called "furqan" (criterion). I say: it is also permissible that the pronoun in "innahu" refers to the statement in which He informed about the resurrection of man on the Day of Resurrection and the testing of his hidden things, meaning: that statement is a definitive statement, conforming to reality, with no jest in it, and the pronoun refers to something mentioned, namely the speech that includes informing about the resurrection, and it is not among the reports in which there is jest, but it is all seriousness.

﴿innahum yakīdūn﴾ (indeed they plot): namely the disbelievers, in nullifying God's command and extinguishing the light of truth. ﴿wa-akīd﴾ (and I plan): I requite them for their plotting. He called the requital "plotting" by way of correspondence, like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they schemed, and God schemed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54], ﴿We are only mockers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], ﴿God mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15]. Then He commanded His Messenger, ﷺ, saying: ﴿So give them respite﴾, meaning: wait for their punishment and do not hasten it. Then He emphasized His command, saying: ﴿give them respite gently﴾, meaning: a respite. When He repeated the command for emphasis, He varied between the two expressions, since the first is unrestricted, and this second is restricted by the phrase ﴿gently﴾. Ibn 'Abbas read: "mahhilhum" (give them respite), with a fatha on the mim and a shadda on the ha', to match the wording of the first command.

When He mentioned that every soul has a guardian over it, He followed this with an exhortation to man to reflect on his first origin, so that he would know that the One who originated him is able to restore him and to requite him. Then he would act accordingly, and would not dictate to his recording angel except what would please him in his final outcome. The phrase ﴿mimma khuliqa﴾ ("from what was he created") [al-Tariq: 5] is an interrogative. "Min" is connected to "khuliqa," and the clause is in the position of an accusative object of "fal-yanzur" ("let him consider"), and it is a suspended clause (mu'allaqah). The answer to the interrogative is what follows it, namely: ﴿He was created from a gushing fluid﴾. This is the semen of the man and the woman. When the two mixed in the womb and became one, He referred to them with "water," which is singular. "Daafiq" (gushing) has been said to mean "madfuq" (poured forth), and this is the reading of Zayd ibn 'Ali. According to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, it is in the relative form (al-nasab), like "laabin" and "taamir," meaning "one who possesses gushing (dafq)." From Ibn 'Abbas: it means "gushing and viscous." It seems that he ascribed to it its attribute, not that it is originally used in the language for this. "Al-dafq" means pouring, and its verb is transitive. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Al-dafq is the pushing of water by some of it against other parts of it, as when a valley or flood 'tadaffaqa' (gushes) when it comes, riding over one another. It is valid that the water is gushing, because some of it pushes others; so some of it is gushing and some of it is poured forth." End of quote. This statement of his was constructed upon "tadaffaqa," and "tadaffaqa" is intransitive; "dafaqtuhu fa-tadaffaqa" is like "kasartuhu fa-takassara" (I broke it, so it broke). But "dafaqa," in the sense he explained, "al-dafq is the pushing of water by some of it against other parts of it," is not in the language; rather, what is preserved is that it means pouring.

The majority read ﴿yakhruju﴾ (comes forth) in the active voice, ﴿min bayn al-sulb﴾ ("from between the loins") with a damma on the ṣād and sukūn on the lām. Ibn Abi 'Abla and Ibn Miqsam read it in the passive voice. They, the people of Mecca, and 'Isa read it with a damma on both the ṣād and the lām. Al-Yamani read it with a fatha on both. Al-'Ajjaj said:

*"In a loin like the well-tanned leather strap"*

The dialects regarding "ṣulb" (loin) have been discussed in the Surah of al-Nisa. Its plural is "ṣalib," as al-'Abbas said:

*"Transferred from a loin to a womb"*

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: its meaning is "from between the loin of each one of the man and the woman and their ribs (tara'ib)." Sufyan and Qatadah also said: "from between the loin of the man and the ribs (tara'ib) of the woman." The explanation of "tara'ib" has already been given in the vocabulary discussion. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the place of the necklace. From Ibn Jubayr: they are the ribs of the man that are below the loin. It was also said: what lies between the two shoulders and the chest. It was said: they are the collarbones. From Ma'mar: it is the essence of the heart, and from it the child comes. Makki transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that the tara'ib are the extremities of a person: his two feet, his two hands, and his two eyes. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "In these conditions, you judge the language." End of quote.

The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ (indeed He) refers to the Creator, who is indicated by "khuliqa" (was created).

﴿'ala raj'ihi﴾ (over his return). Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: the pronoun in "raj'ihi" refers to man, meaning: over his return to life after his death; that is, the One who originated him at first is able to resurrect him on the Day of Resurrection, nothing is beyond Him. Al-Dahhak said: "over his return from old age to youth." 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said: the pronoun refers to the water, meaning over the return of the water into the urethra or into the loin. According to this view and the view of al-Dahhak, the operator (al-'amil) in ﴿yawma tubla﴾ (the Day when hidden things are tested) is an implied verb, its estimated form being "remember." According to the view of Ibn 'Abbas, which is the most apparent, some grammarians said: the operator is "nasir" (helper) from His saying ﴿wa-la nasir﴾ (nor a helper), and this is invalid, because what comes after the "fa" (fa) does not operate on what precedes it, and likewise the negating "ma" does not operate what follows it on what precedes it, according to the well-known and established view. Others, among them al-Zamakhshari, said: the operator is "raj'ihi," but this was refuted on the grounds that it creates a separation between the relative pronoun and its complement, which is part of the relative clause, and this is not permitted. The skilled grammarians said: the operator in it is an implied verb indicated by the verbal noun (masdar), its estimated form being: "He will return him on the Day when hidden things are tested." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "All these groups fled from the operator being 'la-qadir' (is able), because it would appear from this that the power is specified to that day alone. When the meaning and what it requires are considered, the eloquent speech of the Arabs permits that the meaning be 'la-qadir,' because He said: ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾ absolutely, at first and at last, and at every time. Then He mentioned (p. 456) and specified from the times the most important time for the disbelievers, because it is the time of recompense and arrival at punishment, so that people would gather in caution of it and fear of it." End of quote.

﴿tubla﴾ (is tested). It has been said: it is tested. It was said: it is examined, scrutinized, and its good distinguished from its bad. "Al-sara'ir" (hidden things) are what hearts conceal of beliefs and intentions, and what the limbs conceal of deeds. The apparent meaning is the generality of hidden things. In a hadith: "They are monotheism, prayer, zakat, and the ritual bath from major impurity," and what was mentioned in the hadith is the greatest of hidden things. Al-Hasan heard someone reciting:

*"There will remain for her in the hidden part of the heart and the inner chest, a secret affection, on the Day when hidden things are tested."*

He said: "How heedless he is of what is in the sky and the Tariq!" The verse belongs to al-Ahwas.

Since refusal in this world is either by strength within the human being, or by a helper from outside himself, He negated from Himself, may He be exalted, what would prevent Him, and He used "min" (any), which indicates generality, in negating strength and helper.

(By the sky) He swore a second oath by the sky, which is the canopy. It has been said: it may be the clouds.
